tips.title: Common factor first, then look again
tips.body: Take out every common factor, numbers and variables, before anything else: $2x^2 - 8 = 2(x^2 - 4)$. Then read the bracket again, because $x^2 - 4$ is a difference of two squares and *fully* means $2(x - 2)(x + 2)$.

tips.title: A square minus a square, whatever is being squared
tips.body: $a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$ works when $a$ and $b$ are brackets: $(2x + 3)^2 - (2x - 5)^2$ gives $a - b = 8$ and $a + b = 4x - 2$. It also works on numbers: $76^2 - 24^2 = 52 \times 100$.

tips.title: Expand back
tips.body: The only proof a factorisation is right is that it expands to the original. One line, or one substituted value: at $x = 2$, $x^4 - 5x^2 + 4$ is $0$, so $(x - 2)$ must be a factor. A factorisation that expands to something else scores nothing.

tips.title: A fourth power is a quadratic in x²
tips.body: $x^4 - 5x^2 + 4$ is $u^2 - 5u + 4$ with $u = x^2$: factorise the quadratic, then split each difference of two squares. Two rounds, four factors. A sum of two squares such as $x^2 + 4$ stays as it is.

tips.title: Carry y as part of the constant
tips.body: For $15x^2 - 34xy - 16y^2$, $a \times c$ is $15 \times (-16) = -240$, the pair is $-40$ and $6$, and the grouping gives $(5x + 2y)(3x - 8y)$. The method is the one-variable one with $y$ riding along.

why.matters: Factorising is the reverse of expanding, and it is the more valuable direction: a product tells you where an expression is zero, what cancels in a fraction, and what a curve does at its roots, none of which an expanded form shows. GCSE factorised quadratics; Further Maths asks for cubics and fourth powers, two variables, brackets treated as single objects, and the word *fully*, which means every factor has been checked again. The factor theorem, algebraic fractions and the equation of a circle all start by assuming this is quick and reliable, and the exam tests it on its own before it tests it inside them.

examples.title: The mental arithmetic trick
examples.body: Someone who knows $a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$ can do $76^2 - 24^2$ in their head: it is $52 \times 100 = 5200$. The same identity does $49 \times 51$ as $50^2 - 1 = 2499$ and $18^2 - 17^2$ as $1 \times 35 = 35$. It is not a trick so much as the identity read as arithmetic, and it is the clearest demonstration that a factorisation is a statement about numbers, true for every value you put in.

examples.title: Where a curve crosses the axis
examples.body: A graph-plotting app draws $y = x^4 - 5x^2 + 4$ and marks four crossings on the $x$ axis. The expanded form gives no hint where they are; the factorised form $(x - 1)(x + 1)(x - 2)(x + 2)$ names all four at once, because a product is zero exactly when one factor is. Every root of a polynomial is a factor waiting to be found, which is why the factor theorem, the next topic but one, is built on this one and why *factorise fully* matters: an unfound factor is an unfound root.

examples.title: The fraction that will not simplify
examples.body: A student is asked to simplify $\frac{x^2 - 9}{x^2 + 5x + 6}$ and, seeing an $x^2$ on each line, crosses them out. The result is wrong, and one number shows it: at $x = 1$ the original is $-\frac{8}{12}$ and the crossed-out version is $-\frac{9}{11}$. Only a factor of the whole top and the whole bottom can cancel, and factors are found by factorising: $\frac{(x - 3)(x + 3)}{(x + 2)(x + 3)}$ cancels the $(x + 3)$ to leave $\frac{x - 3}{x + 2}$. Factorising is the only way to see what the two lines share.

steps.title: Common factor first, always
steps.body:
*Factorise fully* means keep going until nothing more can be taken out, and the first thing to look for is a **common factor**, including a number. $2x^2 - 8$ has a $2$ in both terms: $2(x^2 - 4)$, and the bracket is a difference of two squares, $2(x - 2)(x + 2)$. Stopping at $2(x^2 - 4)$ is not full, and $(2x - 4)(x + 2)$, which expands correctly, is not full either because $2x - 4$ still holds a $2$.

$3x^2 - 12x + 12 = 3(x^2 - 4x + 4) = 3(x - 2)^2$: the common factor comes out, and what is left is a perfect square. $4x^2 - 12x = 4x(x - 3)$: the common factor can include the variable.

**The habit that earns the last mark:** after factorising, look at every bracket and ask whether it will factorise again. A bracket that is a difference of two squares, a perfect square, or a quadratic with a common factor is not finished.

**The check** is to expand back. $3(x - 2)^2 = 3(x^2 - 4x + 4) = 3x^2 - 12x + 12$. It takes seconds and it is how you know.

check.skill: a common factor then a square
check.solution: The common factor is $3$: $3(x^2 - 4x + 4)$. The bracket is a perfect square, $(x - 2)^2$, so the full factorisation is $3(x - 2)^2$. Check by expanding: $3(x^2 - 4x + 4) = 3x^2 - 12x + 12$.

steps.title: ax² + bx + c, and quadratics in two variables
steps.body:
For $ax^2 + bx + c$ the GCSE method still works: multiply $a$ by $c$, find the pair of numbers that multiply to that and add to $b$, split the middle term, and factorise in pairs. $6x^2 + 7x - 3$: $a \times c = -18$, the pair is $9$ and $-2$, so $6x^2 + 9x - 2x - 3 = 3x(2x + 3) - (2x + 3) = (3x - 1)(2x + 3)$.

The specification adds a **second variable**: factorise $15x^2 - 34xy - 16y^2$. Treat $y$ as part of the constant. $a \times c = 15 \times (-16) = -240$, and the pair that adds to $-34$ is $-40$ and $6$:

$$15x^2 - 40xy + 6xy - 16y^2 = 5x(3x - 8y) + 2y(3x - 8y) = (5x + 2y)(3x - 8y)$$

Every step is the one-variable method with $y$ carried along. The check is the same too: expand $(5x + 2y)(3x - 8y)$ and the middle terms $-40xy + 6xy$ give $-34xy$.

**Finding the pair.** For $-240$, list factor pairs with opposite signs and a difference of $34$: $40$ and $6$ is the one. It is worth writing the pairs down rather than guessing; a wrong pair wastes more time than the list takes.

steps.title: The difference of two squares, in disguise
steps.body:
$a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$, and Further Maths hides the $a$ and $b$. $9x^2 - 16y^2$ is $(3x)^2 - (4y)^2 = (3x - 4y)(3x + 4y)$. $(x + 1)^2 - 4$ is a square minus a square with a whole bracket as $a$: $(x + 1 - 2)(x + 1 + 2) = (x - 1)(x + 3)$.

The specification's example goes one further: **factorise fully** $(2x + 3)^2 - (2x - 5)^2$. Both terms are squares, so

$$\big((2x + 3) - (2x - 5)\big)\big((2x + 3) + (2x - 5)\big) = (8)(4x - 2)$$

and *fully* means the $4x - 2$ gives up its $2$: $8 \times 2(2x - 1) = 16(2x - 1)$.

Expanding both squares and subtracting would reach the same $32x - 16$ in six lines; recognising the pattern does it in two. And the pattern works on numbers: $76^2 - 24^2 = (76 - 24)(76 + 24) = 52 \times 100 = 5200$, without squaring anything.

**What does not factorise.** A **sum** of two squares, $x^2 + 9$, has no factors with real numbers. Knowing that is as much a mark as the factorisation itself, because it stops you inventing $(x + 3)(x + 3)$, which expands to $x^2 + 6x + 9$.

check.prompt: Factorise fully $(2x + 3)^2 - (2x - 5)^2$. The answer has the form $k(2x - 1)$. What is $k$?
check.skill: a difference of two squares with brackets
check.solution: Difference of two squares: $(8)(4x - 2)$. Then $4x - 2 = 2(2x - 1)$, so the full factorisation is $16(2x - 1)$ and $k = 16$.

steps.title: Factorise fully: powers of four
steps.body:
The specification asks for $x^4 - 25x^2$ **factorised fully**. Common factor first: $x^2(x^2 - 25)$. The bracket is a difference of two squares: $x^2(x - 5)(x + 5)$. Three factors, and each is as far as it goes.

$x^4 - 5x^2 + 4$ is a **quadratic in disguise**: with $u = x^2$ it is $u^2 - 5u + 4 = (u - 1)(u - 4)$, so $(x^2 - 1)(x^2 - 4)$, and both brackets are differences of two squares: $(x - 1)(x + 1)(x - 2)(x + 2)$. Four factors from four terms.

$x^4 - 1$ is $(x^2)^2 - 1^2 = (x^2 - 1)(x^2 + 1) = (x - 1)(x + 1)(x^2 + 1)$, and the last bracket stays, because a sum of squares does not factorise.

The pattern in all three: **factorise, then inspect every bracket, then factorise again**. A fourth power usually hides two rounds.

steps.title: Four terms: factorise by grouping
steps.body:
A cubic with four terms and no overall common factor can often be split into two pairs. $x^3 + 2x^2 - 9x - 18$: the first pair has $x^2$ in common, the second has $-9$.

$$x^2(x + 2) - 9(x + 2)$$

The same bracket appears twice, which is the signal that grouping is working, and it becomes a factor: $(x + 2)(x^2 - 9)$. Then the second bracket is a difference of two squares: $(x + 2)(x - 3)(x + 3)$.

**Two things to watch.** Take the sign into the second common factor: it is $-9(x + 2)$, not $9(-x - 2)$, so that the brackets match. And if the brackets do not match, try pairing the terms differently before deciding grouping fails.

**Why it matters.** This is the factorisation the factor theorem topic needs when a cubic has to be solved: $x^3 + 2x^2 - 9x - 18 = 0$ gives $x = -2$, $3$ or $-3$, straight from the three factors.

check.solution: Group: $x^2(x + 2) - 9(x + 2) = (x + 2)(x^2 - 9)$. Then $x^2 - 9 = (x - 3)(x + 3)$, so the full factorisation is $(x + 2)(x - 3)(x + 3)$.

steps.title: Factorising to solve, and factorising to cancel
steps.body:
Factorising is rarely the whole question. It is done in order to **solve** or to **cancel**.

**To solve.** $x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = 0$ becomes $(x - 1)(x + 1)(x - 2)(x + 2) = 0$, and a product is zero only when a factor is, so $x = \pm 1$ or $x = \pm 2$: four solutions, from a quadratic in disguise. The equation is only ever as solvable as the factorisation is complete.

**To cancel.** $\dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x^2 + 5x + 6}$ cannot be simplified until both lines are products: $\dfrac{(x - 3)(x + 3)}{(x + 2)(x + 3)} = \dfrac{x - 3}{x + 2}$. Only a **factor** of the whole top and the whole bottom can be cancelled, never a term; the $x^2$ on each line is a term and cannot go.

Both uses reward the same discipline: factorise fully, check each bracket, and expand back if in doubt. A factorisation that is right but not full leaves solutions unfound and fractions uncancelled.

check.prompt: A student simplifies $\dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x^2 + 5x + 6}$ by cancelling the $x^2$ terms to get $\dfrac{-9}{5x + 6}$. What is wrong?
check.solution: Cancelling works on factors, not terms. Factorise both lines: $\dfrac{(x - 3)(x + 3)}{(x + 2)(x + 3)}$, and the shared factor $(x + 3)$ cancels to leave $\dfrac{x - 3}{x + 2}$. Putting $x = 1$ in shows the student's version is wrong: $\frac{-8}{12}$ against $\frac{-9}{11}$.

steps.title: Going deeper: what "fully" means, and the factorisations that are not there
steps.body:
**Fully is a claim about every bracket.** The mark scheme for *factorise fully* gives the last mark only when no bracket can be factorised further, so the top-band habit is to finish and then read each factor asking three questions: common factor? difference of two squares? perfect square or ordinary quadratic? $x^4 - 5x^2 + 4$ needs the question asked twice; $x^4 - 1$ needs it asked and answered *no* for $x^2 + 1$.

**Know what does not factorise, and say so.** $x^2 + 9$ and $x^2 + 4$ have no real factors: a sum of two squares stays. A quadratic whose $a \times c$ pairs never add to $b$ does not factorise with integers either, and the quadratic formula is the tool then. Writing *does not factorise* with the reason is a mark; inventing brackets that expand to something else loses two.

**Brackets can be $a$ and $b$.** The difference of two squares does not care what is being squared: $(2x + 3)^2 - (2x - 5)^2$ has $a = 2x + 3$ and $b = 2x - 5$, and the $x$ terms cancel in $a - b$ to give a number. Seeing a whole bracket as a single object is the skill the specification is testing with that example.

**Expanding back is not optional.** It is the only proof a factorisation is right, it takes a line, and a top-band answer shows it, or at least checks one value: at $x = 2$, $x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = 16 - 20 + 4 = 0$, so $(x - 2)$ had better be a factor, and it is.

**Where this goes next.** The factor theorem will find one factor of a cubic by substitution and leave you a quadratic to factorise; algebraic fractions will hand you two quadratics to factorise before anything can cancel; and the equation of a circle will need a perfect square recognised on sight. Every one of those topics assumes this one is fast.

steps.title: What to carry forward
steps.body:
- **Common factor first**, including numbers and variables: $2x^2 - 8 = 2(x - 2)(x + 2)$, $3x^2 - 12x + 12 = 3(x - 2)^2$.
- **$ax^2 + bx + c$**: multiply $a$ by $c$, find the pair adding to $b$, split the middle term, group. With a second variable, carry $y$ as part of the constant: $15x^2 - 34xy - 16y^2 = (5x + 2y)(3x - 8y)$.
- **Difference of two squares** $a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$, with $a$ and $b$ possibly brackets: $(2x + 3)^2 - (2x - 5)^2 = 16(2x - 1)$.
- A **sum** of two squares does not factorise.
- **Fourth powers** take two rounds: $x^4 - 25x^2 = x^2(x - 5)(x + 5)$; $x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = (x - 1)(x + 1)(x - 2)(x + 2)$.
- **Four terms**: group in pairs, extract the repeated bracket: $x^3 + 2x^2 - 9x - 18 = (x + 2)(x - 3)(x + 3)$.
- **Fully** means every bracket has been checked again.
- Factorise to **solve** (each factor to zero) and to **cancel** (factors only, never terms).
- **Expand back** to check.

questions.prompt: Which of these does not factorise with real numbers?
questions.solution: A sum of two squares has no real factors. $x^2 - 9 = (x - 3)(x + 3)$, $x^2 + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)^2$ and $9x^2 - 1 = (3x - 1)(3x + 1)$ all factorise; $x^2 + 9$ does not, and $(x + 3)^2$ is wrong because it expands to $x^2 + 6x + 9$.
Difference of two squares with $a = 2x + 3$ and $b = 2x - 5$: $(a - b)(a + b) = (8)(4x - 2)$. Fully: $8 \times 2(2x - 1) = 16(2x - 1)$.
$a \times c = -240$, and the pair adding to $-34$ is $-40$ and $6$. Split: $15x^2 - 40xy + 6xy - 16y^2 = 5x(3x - 8y) + 2y(3x - 8y) = (5x + 2y)(3x - 8y)$.

questions.prompt: A student factorises $x^4 - 25x^2$ as $x^2(x^2 - 25)$ and stops. Why does this lose the last mark?
questions.solution: *Fully* means every bracket is checked again. $x^2 - 25$ is $x^2 - 5^2$, a difference of two squares, so the factorisation continues to $x^2(x - 5)(x + 5)$. $(x - 5)^2$ is wrong: it expands to $x^2 - 10x + 25$.

questions.prompt:
(a) Factorise fully $x^4 - 5x^2 + 4$.

(b) Hence solve $x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = 0$.

(c) A student says that $x^4 + 5x^2 + 4$ has the same number of real solutions when set equal to zero. Show that the student is wrong.
questions.solution:
**(a)** The expression is a quadratic in $x^2$: writing $u = x^2$ gives $u^2 - 5u + 4$, and two numbers that multiply to $4$ and add to $-5$ are $-1$ and $-4$. So $(x^2 - 1)(x^2 - 4)$. Both brackets are differences of two squares, and *fully* means they must be split: $(x - 1)(x + 1)(x - 2)(x + 2)$.

**(b)** A product is zero only when a factor is zero, so $x - 1 = 0$, $x + 1 = 0$, $x - 2 = 0$ or $x + 2 = 0$: $x = 1, -1, 2$ or $-2$. Four solutions, one from each factor. Check one: $x = 2$ gives $16 - 20 + 4 = 0$.

**(c)** $x^4 + 5x^2 + 4$ is also a quadratic in $x^2$: two numbers multiplying to $4$ and adding to $5$ are $1$ and $4$, so it factorises as $(x^2 + 1)(x^2 + 4)$. Each bracket is a **sum** of two squares, which does not factorise further, and neither can equal zero for a real number: $x^2$ is never negative, so $x^2 + 1 \geqslant 1$ and $x^2 + 4 \geqslant 4$. The equation $x^4 + 5x^2 + 4 = 0$ therefore has **no** real solutions, against four for the original. Changing the sign of the middle term changed the differences of two squares into sums, and that is the whole difference.

Both brackets are differences of two squares, and *fully* means they must be split: $(x - 1)(x + 1)(x - 2)(x + 2)$.

**(b)** A product is zero only when a factor is zero, so $x - 1 = 0$, $x + 1 = 0$, $x - 2 = 0$ or $x + 2 = 0$: $x = 1, -1, 2$ or $-2$. Four solutions, one from each factor. Check one: $x = 2$ gives $16 - 20 + 4 = 0$.

**(c)** $x^4 + 5x^2 + 4$ is also a quadratic in $x^2$: two numbers multiplying to $4$ and adding to $5$ are $1$ and $4$, so it factorises as $(x^2 + 1)(x^2 + 4)$. Each bracket is a **sum** of two squares, which does not factorise further, and neither can equal zero for a real number: $x^2$ is never negative, so $x^2 + 1 \geqslant 1$ and $x^2 + 4 \geqslant 4$. The equation $x^4 + 5x^2 + 4 = 0$ therefore has **no** real solutions, against four for the original. Changing the sign of the middle term changed the differences of two squares into sums, and that is the whole difference.

questions.prompt:
(a) Factorise fully $(2x + 3)^2 - (2x - 5)^2$.

(b) Factorise fully $x^3 + 2x^2 - 9x - 18$.

(c) Hence write down the solutions of $x^3 + 2x^2 - 9x - 18 = 0$.
questions.skill: the specification's difference of two squares, and grouping
questions.solution:
**(a)** Both terms are squares, so use $a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$ with $a = 2x + 3$ and $b = 2x - 5$.

$a - b = (2x + 3) - (2x - 5) = 2x + 3 - 2x + 5 = 8$.

$a + b = (2x + 3) + (2x - 5) = 4x - 2$.

So the expression is $8(4x - 2)$. That is not yet full, because $4x - 2 = 2(2x - 1)$: the answer is $16(2x - 1)$. Expanding both squares and subtracting gives $32x - 16$, which agrees.

**(b)** Four terms and no overall common factor, so group in pairs: $(x^3 + 2x^2) + (-9x - 18) = x^2(x + 2) - 9(x + 2)$. The bracket $(x + 2)$ appears in both, so it is a factor: $(x + 2)(x^2 - 9)$. Then $x^2 - 9$ is a difference of two squares: $(x + 2)(x - 3)(x + 3)$.

**(c)** A product is zero only when a factor is, so $x + 2 = 0$, $x - 3 = 0$ or $x + 3 = 0$: the solutions are $x = -2$, $x = 3$ and $x = -3$. *Hence* means they are to be read from part (b), not found afresh; a check by substitution confirms one of them, since $x = 3$ gives $27 + 18 - 27 - 18 = 0$.

examTechnique.body:
*Factorise fully* is marked in stages, and the last mark is for the word **fully**: a common factor left inside a bracket, or a difference of two squares left unsplit, loses it. So finish, then read every bracket again with three questions: common factor, difference of two squares, a quadratic that splits.

For $ax^2 + bx + c$, write the pair for $a \times c$ down rather than guessing, and carry a second variable as part of the constant. For a square minus a square, name $a$ and $b$ even when they are brackets, and expect $a - b$ to be short. For four terms, group. And **expand back** before moving on; it is the only check that proves anything, and it costs a line.
examinerErrors: Stopping at $x^2(x^2 - 25)$ or $2(x^2 - 4)$ when *fully* was asked.
Leaving a common factor inside a bracket: $(2x - 4)(x + 2)$ for $2x^2 - 8$.
Inventing factors for a sum of two squares, such as $(x + 3)(x + 3)$ for $x^2 + 9$.
Getting the pair for $a \times c$ wrong and not checking by expanding.
Losing the sign when grouping, so the two brackets do not match.
Cancelling a **term** across a fraction instead of a factor.
Treating $(2x + 3)^2 - (2x - 5)^2$ by expanding both squares and making an arithmetic slip, when the difference of two squares does it in two lines.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer takes the common factor first, factorises what is left, and then reads every bracket again until *fully* is true, including the second round that a fourth power hides. It sees $(2x + 3)^2 - (2x - 5)^2$ as a square minus a square with brackets for $a$ and $b$, and writes $16(2x - 1)$ in two lines. It carries a second variable through the splitting method without fuss, groups a four-term cubic and extracts the repeated bracket, and says when a sum of two squares stays as it is, with the reason. It expands back, or substitutes a value, as a matter of habit, and when the factorisation is being done in order to solve or to cancel, it goes on to do that with every factor accounted for.
